title: Bicycle Acrobatics with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Bicycle robots are fast and energy efficient, but their simple mechanical design and their underactuated and non-holonomic dynamics make highly agile maneuvers difficult to achieve. Here, we use Reinforcement Learning (RL) to enable a bicycle robot to learn and compose a diverse repertoire of dynamic acrobatic stunts. Using different RL formulations such as waypoint following, pose reaching, twist tracking, guided tracking, and motion imitation, the robot acquires autonomous single and multi-table forward and lateral jumps, steerable jumps, front flips, kip-ups, kip-downs, driving, wheelies, bunny hops, and three-point turns. To coordinate these behaviors, we introduce an orchestrator that transitions between policies using state-dependent triggers, enabling robust long-horizon acrobatic stunts. We validate the approach on the Ultra Mobility Vehicle (UMV), a custom bicycle robot, in simulation and hardware. The robot repeatedly traverses tables up to 1 m high, performs more than 15 consecutive autonomous jumps while following waypoints, handles previously unseen multi-table configurations, executes continuous repertoires of kipups, jumps, flips, kip-downs, over more than 20 consecutive trials, and performs more than 10 consecutive autonomous and steerable repertoires of wheelies, lateral jumps, and single-wheel jump downs. These results demonstrate that RL can endow bicycle robots with levels of agility previously associated primarily with legged platforms while preserving the speed and efficiency of wheeled locomotion, establishing a foundation for bicycle acrobatics.

title: A Data-Driven Framework For UAV Trajectory Prediction And Abnormal Motion Detection Using Remote ID Telemetry
abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems are increasingly being adopted across commercial, industrial, and autonomous applications, creating a growing demand for intelligent monitoring techniques that improve operational safety, situational awareness, and airspace management. Among recent research directions in UAV systems, trajectory analysis and behavior monitoring have become essential for supporting reliable and scalable UAV operations. This thesis investigates two complementary challenges in UAV monitoring: trajectory prediction and abnormal motion-deviation detection.The first part of this thesis focuses on UAV trajectory prediction under incomplete observation conditions. A deep learning framework was developed to estimate future UAV positions using historical flight information and maintain trajectory continuity during periods of missing or interrupted telemetry data. Multiple deep learning models, including a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Transformer, were implemented and evaluated using real-world UAV trajectory datasets. Experimental results demonstrated that sequence-based models consistently outperformed non-temporal models by more effectively capturing temporal dependencies, leading to more accurate future trajectory prediction. The second part of this thesis presents a comparative framework for detecting abnormal UAV motion deviations using large-scale Remote ID telemetry data. Motion descriptors representing speed, acceleration, altitude, heading, and their temporal variations were extracted and organized into fixed-length sliding windows to characterize short-term UAV dynamics. Because the RID datasets do not contain verified abnormal motion labels, a controlled motion-deviation injection methodology was developed to generate reproducible benchmark datasets while preserving realistic flight behavior. Within this unified framework, three complementary detection approaches were evaluated: a statistical threshold-based detector, an MLP Autoencoder, and a Transformer Autoencoder. The statistical detector provides an interpretable and computationally efficient baseline, whereas the AI-based autoencoders learn normal UAV motion patterns and detect deviations using reconstruction error. Experimental results demonstrated that the MLP Autoencoder achieved the highest overall F1-score, while the Transformer Autoencoder provided the highest detection sensitivity through temporal sequence modeling. Although the statistical approach remained computationally efficient and highly interpretable, its reliance on fixed thresholds limited its ability to detect complex motion deviations, demonstrating the advantages of learning-based methods for UAV motion-deviation detection. Together, the two proposed frameworks address both predictive and diagnostic aspects of intelligent UAV monitoring by estimating future UAV motion and detecting abnormal motion deviations from Remote ID telemetry. The combined outcomes of this thesis establish a comprehensive data-driven approach that improves UAV situational awareness and operational reliability while supporting future applications in Remote ID surveillance, autonomous traffic management, collision avoidance, and large-scale airspace monitoring.

title: Man, Machine, and Simulation: A Theoretical Framework Towards AGI with Experimentations
abstract: Major advances in artificial intelligence have repeatedly promised general intelligence, yet each paradigm has encountered architectural limits. Despite rapid progress, the architectures, environments, and evaluation methods sufficient for artificial general intelligence (AGI) remain uncertain. This thesis proposes a neurocognitively inspired framework, defined at the computational and algorithmic levels of Marr’s analysis, to guide and assess AGI research. It reviews state-of-the-art vision-language models (VLMs) and world models, then introduces two hybrid architectures combining the semantic understanding of VLMs with the physical modeling capabilities of world models. These systems are evaluated in two-dimensional discrete and three-dimensional continuous environments, with future extensions to broader tasks. The thesis further argues that social simulations are essential AGI testbeds because they support open-ended environments, complex roles, multi-agent coordination, and emergent behavior under increasingly realistic social, cognitive, and physical constraints. Such simulations enable reciprocal human–AI learning, safety assessment, and applications in the real world.

title: Intelligent Life Science Research
abstract: Currently, research in the fields of general artificial intelligence and bionic robotics lacks a unified underlying theoretical framework. Existing large models and bionic robots cannot explain the unified mechanisms of recognition, thinking, control, emotion, and learning for either biological life or electromechanical artificial life. This paper establishes a comprehensive theoretical system of intelligent life science: it defines life uniformly as a machine capable of self-maintenance and possessing skill-processing functions; constructs a minimal innate intelligent life model, dividing life forms into a dual structure of "innate hardware and innate algorithms — all self-acquired skills"; and proposes three core laws of acquired skills and their corresponding algorithms, namely the Representation Law (associative structure, skill representation and storage), Learning Law (skill discovery and propagation), and Activation Law (skill application), which standardize the data structures and processing algorithms for the four fundamental abilities of recognition, thinking, control, and desire/emotion. These three laws are objective laws independently discovered by the author. All animals comply with these three laws, and the corresponding algorithms form the only foundational algorithms for animal intelligence computation. Artificial machines can also run the corresponding three algorithms, enabling machines to become intelligent and agile through acquired experience just like animals. The algorithms provided in this paper support the creation of general intelligent life (machines). In practical engineering, discarding all existing mainstream algorithms, manufacturing under the guidance of this theory does not require preset programs for recognition, control, language, consciousness, or any other specific functional code. All functionalities arise from acquired non-intrusive learning (exploration and communication). This paper further clarifies that the original driving force (source of desire) is the sole origin of autonomous behavior in life forms, explaining the mechanisms of all intelligent phenomena; it proposes two technological pathways for the perpetual survival of humanity and suggests the possibility that intelligent life could be the ultimate engineering project in human scientific endeavors. It discovers the theoretical equivalence between organic biological life and inorganic electromechanical artificial life, providing a complete and implementable engineering paradigm for humanoid autonomous robots, growable artificial life, consciousness transfer, and fully autonomous general intelligent systems. This paper includes the principles and manufacturing theories for implementable engineering intelligent life with empty innate skills, capable of acquiring any skills later, and possessing autonomous goals.

title: Multilingual Intermediate Task Fine-Tuning for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer in XLM-R
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: Does fine-tuning XLM-R with multilingual intermediate tasks (e.g., TyDiQA, MLQA) improve zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on XTREME-R compared to English-only intermediate tasks, as measured by F1 score across all languages and tasks? title: From Harness to cognitive runtime: an architectural hypothesis of control plane for AI systems—a theory of cognitive governance toward artificial general intelligence
abstract: The engineering practice of large language models (LLMs) and Agent systems is currently facing a structural dilemma: seemingly disparate technical approaches, such as LangGraph, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and Guardrail, are all optimizing execution efficiency on the same "cognitive map", yet they universally lack a meta-cognitive capability to determine whether the current cognitive map itself remains valid. This study argues that this dilemma is not accidental but a structurally inclined manifestation of the "compression-residual" structure inherent in any finite cognitive system under long-term operation and continuous environmental adaptation. To address this, an architectural theory of cognitive runtime is proposed. The core thesis is that LLMs generate cognitive content, while the cognitive runtime manages the lifecycle of cognitive states. The main contributions include: ① proposing "complexity-capability divergence (CCD)" as a working concept for diagnosing the long-term evolutionary trajectory of cognitive systems, and clarifying its distinction from existing concepts such as concept drift and technical debt; ② revealing that the fundamental driving force behind the continuous expansion of Harness systems is the misalignment between token loss and business loss objectives, and pointing out that scaling optimizes the accuracy of selection among existing frameworks rather than the meta-selection capability of deciding whether to abandon the current framework; ③ presenting a systematic definition of the cognitive runtime—a system layer responsible for creating, maintaining, evaluating, migrating, and reorganizing the lifecycle of cognitive states—and arguing for its plausibility and principled justification as an independent system layer; ④ outlining the possible evolutionary path of the cognitive runtime from "state maintenance" to "ontological evolution", and clarifying the role of humans as value boundary setters and paradigm supervisors within this architecture. The core contribution of this paper is not to propose a new Agent framework, but to abstract "cognitive framework switching" as an independently manageable runtime behavior, and thereby to propose the cognitive runtime as a new system layer. This study presents a testable theoretical hypothesis and provides five falsifiable predictions. The mathematical representation and evolutionary algorithms of cognitive state space remain open questions. The aim of this paper is to provide a discussable, revisable, and falsifiable conceptual framework for future research.

title: Quantitative Assessment and Verification of Quantum Neural Network Security Based on Violations of the Bell Inequality
abstract: In response to the current research landscape, which lacks unified quantitative standards and a reproducible verification framework for assessing the security of quantum neural networks (QNNs), this paper proposes a quantitative evaluation system and verification scheme for QNN security based on the violation characteristics of CHSH-type Bell inequalities. This method treats quantum entanglement as the core element of intrinsic security and establishes a controlled-variable controlled experiment involving purely classical models, non-entangled QNNs, weakly entangled QNNs, and strongly entangled QNNs. Numerical simulations were conducted using the Iris dataset; the presence of quantum entanglement was determined using the CHSH statistic, and a quantitative metric system centered on the normalized CHSH observation metric Q was constructed. Based on the theoretical limits of Bell's inequalities, a normalization derivation was performed to establish the theoretical constraint interval of 0≤Q≤1; the threshold values of 0.3 and 0.7 obtained from the simulations are applicable only to the experimental scenarios described in this paper and serve solely as a reference for grouping data within the experiment; they do not possess universal validity for determination. Simulation results show that the CHSH values for the weakly and strongly entangled QNN experimental groups can reach 2.8284, significantly exceeding the theoretical limits of classical locality. These values correspond to an observation metric of Q=0.9838 and a privacy protection strength of P=0.8854, with the security level rated as high. The CHSH values of the non-entangled QNN and the purely classical model do not exceed the classical threshold of 2; they exhibit no quantum nonlocality or quantum advantage, and their security level is rated as low. This paper advances the security evaluation of QNNs from qualitative, empirical judgments to verifiable quantitative classification, providing a theoretical basis and evaluation framework for the practical application of quantum neural networks in highly security-sensitive scenarios such as privacy-preserving computing.

title: Consumer cognitive and emotion driven personalised artificial intelligence; A mixed method of factor analysis through SOR theory
abstract: The rapid integration of personalised artificial intelligence (AI) into digital platforms has fundamentally transformed consumer decision-making by simultaneously engaging cognitive evaluations and emotional responses. Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S-O-R) theory, this study investigates how personalised AI systems function as external stimuli that shape consumers’ internal cognitive and emotional states, ultimately influencing behavioural outcomes. Using a quantitative research design, data were collected from 120 consumers in urban settings through a structured questionnaire measured on a five-point Likert scale. Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) was employed to identify the underlying dimensions of consumer responses toward personalised AI. The Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin value (0.822) and Bartlett’s Test of Sphericity (χ² = 3086.999, df = 435, p < 0.001) confirmed the adequacy of the data for factor analysis. The results revealed a robust six-factor structure explaining consumer responses to personalised AI: cognitive trust and transparency, perceived control and autonomy, privacy concern and intrusiveness, cognitive efficiency and decision support, behavioural intention and platform loyalty, and emotional engagement and affective response. The findings demonstrate that consumer acceptance and continued use of personalised AI systems are jointly driven by rational cognitive assessments and affective experiences rather than functional efficiency alone. The study contributes to AI-driven consumer behaviour literature by empirically extending the S-O-R framework to personalised AI contexts and offers practical insights for designing transparent, user-centric, and emotionally intelligent AI systems that foster trust, engagement, and long-term loyalty.

title: Beyond the Knowledge Frontier: An Epistemological Framework for Marketing Strategy in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Artificial intelligence represents a fundamental disruption to marketing, yet existing research treats AI as an instrumental tool rather than an epistemological challenge. This paper makes an original theoretical contribution by reframing AI's impact as an epistemological transformation rather than solely as an adoption decision. Introducing a four-quadrant knowledge matrix distinguishing known knowns, known unknowns, unknown unknowns, and unknown knowns, the analysis reveals that AI amplifies exploitation of known knowns through automation, accelerates exploration of known unknowns through analytics, but paradoxically both reveals and generates unknown unknowns through emergent behaviors that reorganize markets unpredictably. Traditional uncertainty-reduction strategies prove inadequate for these inherently unpredictable disruptions. Building on Taleb's concept of antifragility, the paper argues marketing organizations should shift from knowledge optimization toward epistemic antifragility. The goal is to provide scholars with new frameworks for theorizing uncertainty under AI disruption, while offering managers and policymakers actionable guidance for building organizational capabilities that gain strength from disruption rather than simply attempting to eliminate it.

title: Privacy-preserving hierarchical federated learning via CKKS homomorphic encryption
abstract: Hierarchical federated learning (HFL) reduces cloud-facing traffic by aggregating client updates at intermediate edge servers, but plaintext aggregation exposes model updates to honest-but-curious infrastructure. This paper studies a client–edge–cloud HFL architecture protected by the Cheon–Kim–Kim–Song (CKKS) approximate homomorphic-encryption scheme and evaluated under wireless impairments. Clients encrypt packed model updates, edge servers aggregate ciphertexts, and the cloud completes the second aggregation stage without accessing plaintext updates. A trusted key holder alone decrypts the global update. The wireless model accounts for heterogeneous bandwidth, fading, packet loss, retransmissions, and deadline-based client admission. Experiments on Fashion-MNIST use 20 clients, four edge servers, Dirichlet non-IID partitioning with concentration α = 0.5 , and 100 global rounds. Four variants are compared: plaintext HFL, CKKS-HFL, wireless plaintext HFL, and wireless CKKS-HFL. Under reliable links, plaintext and CKKS curves nearly overlap and exceed 91% final accuracy, while CKKS relative aggregation error remains below approximately 6 × 1 0 − 10 in the ideal-link case. Wireless plaintext HFL remains close to the reliable-link baseline because almost all clients are received each round. In contrast, wireless CKKS-HFL admits only about one to seven clients per round because encrypted updates are much larger, causing noisier convergence and lower final accuracy of approximately 89%. HFL nevertheless reduces encrypted edge-to-cloud traffic from roughly 670 MB at the client tier to about 470 MB in the ideal CKKS case, with larger reductions when wireless admission limits participation. These results show that CKKS numerical error is negligible, whereas ciphertext-induced communication pressure is the dominant practical bottleneck.

title: Causal Inference with Unstructured Treatments
abstract: Causal inference usually concerns a scalar treatment, yet in many problems the treatment is unstructured: a text, an image, or a sequence of clinical decisions. Consider an instructor writing a course description to attract more students: the treatment is the course description, and the outcome is enrollment. The standard target, the average treatment effect of fixing the treatment to one exact value versus another, runs into two problems. It cannot be estimated, because almost no exact description recurs across courses, leaving no comparable group from which to measure its effect; and it would be of little use even if it could, since no one wants every course to carry the same description. What the instructor actually wants to know is which features of a description raise enrollment, and which of those features can be acted on across many courses. To this end, we propose a causal query for unstructured treatments: the maximally influential feature (MIF), the feature of the treatment that most strongly influences the outcome. We formalize the MIF as a binary feature of the treatment, defined by a feature-scoring function, constrained so that both of its values stay well populated, and chosen to maximize the causal effect it induces. Turning the feature on shifts the distribution of treatments toward those that display it, turning it off shifts away, and the MIF effect contrasts the two average potential outcomes. We study identification conditions for the MIF, develop algorithms to estimate it, and make it actionable through a nudging algorithm that revises a treatment along the MIF into an outcome-improving version. We illustrate the MIF algorithm across applications in text, image, and dynamic treatment sequences.

title: Artificial General Intelligence: Principles and Practices
abstract: As the role of artificial intelligence grows in our everyday lives, so does the need for AI with greater capabilities. Unlike narrow AI, confined to specific tasks, artificial general intelligence seeks human-like adaptability, reasoning, and learning across domains. Integrating cognitive, mathematical, and computational concepts, it presents multidimensional solutions to create more natural human-AI interactions. This book examines the theoretical foundations, cognitive architectures, and practical methodologies shaping artificial general intelligence. It highlights the significance of human-like emotional intelligence in AI and its potential to create more natural, empathetic, and intuitive human-AI interactions, using techniques such as facial expression analysis, speech emotion recognition, and physiological signal processing. From healthcare to customer service, affective AI is being used to enhance user experiences by tailoring interactions to the emotional states of individuals. The book also discusses the ethical dilemmas posed by affective AI, such as emotional manipulation, bias in emotion detection, and the impact of AI-driven emotional decisions on human behavior. Balancing rigor with practical insight, the volume provides a roadmap for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers to study artificial general intelligence’s evolution and transformative potential. [From the publisher]

title: Building Trustworthy AI Systems: Explainable Decision Support, Privacy-Preserving Learning, and Agentic Federated Workflows
abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence, particularly large language models (LLMs), has created new opportunities for deploying intelligent systems in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and education. At the same time, practical adoption remains constrained by several persistent challenges, including the need for trustworthy and explainable decision support, the protection of sensitive data, and the difficulty of training robust models under heterogeneous and decentralized data conditions. This dissertation addresses these challenges through three complementary studies that develop AI frameworks integrating explainable machine learning, knowledge-augmented LLMs, agentic AI, federated learning, and privacy-preserving data processing for medical and educational applications. The first study develops an explainable AI framework for clinical decision support. Although existing explainable machine learning methods can reveal useful information about model behavior, their outputs are often technical and difficult for healthcare practitioners to interpret directly. To bridge this gap, the proposed framework combines model-agnostic explanations with knowledge-augmented LLMs. Binary classifiers are trained for clinical depression diagnosis using biological indicators, and explanation-related information is organized into a structured knowledge graph that preserves explanatory evidence and captures relationships among models, features, predictions, and explanation patterns. A graph-based retrieval-augmented generation architecture enables practitioners to explore model behavior through natural language dialogue. The system is further enhanced with Long Chain-of-Thought training, which allows complex practitioner questions to be decomposed into sub-questions that can each be addressed through targeted retrieval. Through this design, the framework translates technical model explanations into accessible, domain-relevant responses that help practitioners evaluate model behavior and trustworthiness. The second study proposes Agent-Orchestrated Federated Representation Learning, a collaborative learning framework designed for heterogeneous and decentralized data environments. Inspired by federated learning, the framework leverages agentic AI to automate coordination among distributed clients while reducing the need to exchange raw data or full model parameters. Client-side encoders extract privacy-protected feature representations, and controlled noise is added locally before upload. Through multi-agent communication, a server agent dynamically coordinates client contributions using per-class budget allocation, improving class coverage and adaptation under non-independent and identically distributed data conditions. Experiments on CIFAR-100 demonstrate that the proposed approach improves accuracy, convergence speed, communication efficiency, and long-tail class performance compared with standard federated learning baselines. These results show the potential of agentic AI to improve privacy-sensitive collaborative learning in heterogeneous data settings. The third study examines the use of LLMs for programming education, with a focus on privacy-preserving Java code assessment and correction. A dataset of more than 1,500 Java programming tasks was curated, standardized, and manually reviewed, with programming errors categorized into syntax, runtime, and logical errors. Based on this dataset, the proposed framework learns to identify programming mistakes and generate meaningful explanations and corrective feedback. This study demonstrates the potential of LLM-based systems to support programming assessment while addressing the need to protect sensitive student submissions. Taken together, this dissertation demonstrates how explainable AI, LLM-enabled natural language interaction, agentic coordination, privacy-preserving learning, and carefully curated domain-specific datasets can support more transparent, adaptive, efficient, and practically deployable AI systems for sensitive applications in healthcare and education and for decentralized learning under heterogeneous data conditions.

title: A Threshold-Optimized Hybrid Ensemble for imbalanced Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Restaurant Reviews
abstract: Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) is a vital method for extracting detailed opinions from customer feedback, but current approaches often overlook important factors such as menu variety and struggle with class imbalance in real-world data. This research propose a hybrid lexical-probabilistic ensemble system that combines SentiWordNet lexical resources with a dual-branch Naïve Bayes ensemble, using Multinomial Naïve Bayes for text features and Gaussian Naïve Bayes for continuous lexical sentiment features, to enhance accuracy across five restaurant aspects: food quality, service, physical environment, price fairness, and menu variety. The study was evaluated on 10,000 Kaggle restaurant reviews. After excluding neutral reviews, the remaining binary dataset was imbalanced, and evaluation was performed using a stratified 80:20 train–test split. Dataset preprocessing through tokenization, lemmatization, and stop-word removal was applied, and aspect extraction was also performed using domain-specific keyword dictionaries enriched with WordNet synonyms, Part-of-Speech tagging, and dependency parsing, while SentiWordNet assigned aspect-level sentiment scores. A threshold optimization strategy was applied to the posterior probabilities of the positive class to improve minority-class recall while maintaining overall precision without harming majority class performance. Results show that the ensemble achieves 86% precision, 80% recall, and 82% F1-score, significantly outperforming basic classifiers such as standalone Naïve Bayes, SentiWordNet-augmented Naïve Bayes, and a hybrid ELMo-Wikipedia method. Statistical tests with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test confirm these improvements (p < 1.91e-06). This framework provides fine-grained aspect-level sentiment analytics for restaurant decision support and lays a solid groundwork for handling imbalanced sentiment analysis. Future work discusses integrating transformer-based models and multilingual support. Keywords: Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis, Class Imbalance, Customer Satisfaction, Ensemble Learning, Naïve Bayes Classifier, Restaurant Reviews, SentiWordNet, Threshold Optimization
